items.title: Curtis Sittenfeld’s Prep is coming to the small screen. Who should play Lee?
items.summary:
Back in 2005, Curtis Sittenfeld’s debut novel Prep was the talk of the town. We debated everything from its genre to its striving protagonist, whose moral universe felt like something straight outta Wharton. Sittenfeld was praised and derided for her frankness about class and adolescent sex.

21 years later, this ur-Millennial text has finally gotten a green-light from Hollywood. A buzzy new adaptation helmed by the One Day team is coming soon to a Netflix near you —but we don’t yet have the skinny on casting. Which is where I come in.

The benefit of being a reader moonlighting in theatre is a certain—if I do say so myself—knack for casting. Here are some terrific young actors working today who would do that vexing protagonist justice.

*

Lee Fiora, Prep’ s heroine, is a heartland daughter with her soul set on a tony East Coast boarding school.

We learn in the novel that she’s a white brunette with romantic notions. At school, she hopes to “ meet a melancholy, athletic boy ” who also likes reading and sweaters. But once Lee arrives at the austere Ault academy, a lot of that dreaminess goes right out the window.

It’s a tricky brief for a young actor. One has to drive a story, but from a passive place. My colleague McKayla Coyle pitched the up-and-coming Ella Rubin as a natural fit for the challenge.

Rubin previously wowed streaming audiences on Sterling Point from Amazon Prize, and has since stolen scenes in Sean Baker joints.

She’s generally captivating onscreen, but I think one of her performances captures Lee’s striver contradictions especially well. Her misguided…

items.title: The 2026 Cercador Prize goes to The Song of Stork and Dromedary.
items.summary:
Today, the Cercador Prize announced David McKay as the winner of the 2026 prize for his translation of Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary , published by Two Lines Press.

“Even amongst this year’s impressive finalists, The Song of Stork and Dromedary overwhelmed the committee in its ambition,” this year’s jury, chaired by Pierce Alquist of Brookline Booksmith, said in a statement.

Inspired by the Brontë sisters, Emily in particular, the novel weaves interconnected stories, letters, diary entries, and more to explore the life and expansive afterlives of a writer and her work. McKay’s translation captures all that is wild and beautiful in the novel, from its stunning prose and the chilling setting of the Yorkshire moors, to every multilayered element and form, masterfully rendering changes in language over the span of 200 years. It is a staggering achievement.

McKay will receive a $1,000 award for the prize. He is an award-winning translator of Dutch fiction and nonfiction and his previous translations include Anjet Daanje’s The Remembered Soldier , Off-White by Astrid Roemer, and the award-winning War and Turpentine by Stefan Hertmans. Born and educated in the United States, he has lived in and around The Hague since 1997.

In addition to Alquist, this year’s Cercador jury included Sophie Chen of Belmont Books (Belmont, MA), Mikayla Bryant of Books Are Magic (Brooklyn, NY), Lou Barcott of Myopic Books (Chicago, IL), and James Webster of Recluse Books (Fort Worth, TX) and the shortlist included translations from Jeffrey Zuckerman, Izidora Angel, Saskia Vogel,…
items.t: The 2026 Cercador Prize goes to The Song of Stork and Dromedary.

items.title: The 10 Best Picture Books of 2026, According to the NYT and NYPL

For 2026, the judges were children’s librarian Kelly-Ann Smith, children’s author Julie Fogliano, and children’s author/illustrator Edel Rodriguez. While We’re Here , written by Anne Wynter and illustrated by Micha Archer 
 “Archer’s cut-paper collage illustrations match the tempo of the story in the way a musical score relates to the action of a film.”

items.title: Ali Hazelwood Sparks Discourse About White Authors Writing Black Characters
items.summary:
Romance author Ali Hazelwood, best known for The Love Hypothesis , sparked a lot of discussion over the weekend after hosting a Q&A on her subreddit. To promote her new Audible-only romance Bad in Bed , Ali Hazelwood did an Ask Me Anything on r/AliHazelwood, through the official Audible account. One of the questions she was asked was, “Do you plan on writing a book with Black main characters?” This was her answer:

I have no plans to write a Black FMC. Aside from the usual considerations about whether that can be done well by a white author (sorry, not that I’m setting these considerations aside because they’re not important, just beause it’s such a big conversation to have and this is prob. not the best format) I just think that publishing is not investing and uplifting enough Black stories written by Black writers, and I would hate for my (lbr, very limited) take on the Black experience to be the one that sucks up resources from them. (And also some of my fave Black romance writers: Shirlene Obuobi, Nikki Payne, Adriana Herrera, Claire Kann, Tia Williams, Kennedy Ryan, Alexa Martin, OH GOD I KNOW I AM FORGETTING SOME AND I WILL WAKE UP SWEATY AT 3 AM HATING MYSELF FOR IT)

She also answered a question about whether Nyota Fuli, a Black side character in Not In Love , would be getting a book to herself by saying that she didn’t think she’d write a book with a Black female main character, but she would love to partner with a Black writer and write the male main character’s perspective.

Her answers started a discussion on X/Twitter, which quickly spread to TikTok and other…

items.title: I Want to Have a Baby Because I Miss the Violence
items.summary:
An excerpt from Nanny Nanny by K Chiucarello 

I had a feeling this was coming when Michael began texting heavily a few days ago. On the first snow of the season, he texted to say he’d had a dream about Jenny.

You know your friend Jenny? he asked me.

Jenny, as in my best friend? I replied.

Exactly, he said.

In the dream Jenny had gotten a tattoo of a tampon on the back of her leg, right in the ditch behind the knee, which I hear is one of the most painful body parts to place something permanent. Michael thought it was funny and specific that Jenny had appeared to him in the night and that a tampon was involved.

He texted, Do you remember telling me about those, about periods and the smell of rust that hits the nose when a flood opens like that?

In high school, I had been the first to teach him all about tampons. We were in his Buick when I explained to him all the chores women must suffer through when they begin their periods. There’s ruined jeans, I told him, and heating pads, long hours of lying horizontal or moving through the world with cotton shoved into you. A string. A metallic smell, I said, crinkling my poreless face. Here, I said, leaning over to Michael from the passenger seat. Smell this. And I shoved a fake gold bracelet my mother had purchased for me into his nose.

It’s certainly a smell, he replied, reclining back into the driver’s seat.

So. Michael had this dream about Jenny getting a tampon tattoo and he texted me, coming back into my life like clockwork, like he does every season.

We never could stop speaking for good, despite both of us acting,…

items.title: Work Up an Appetite with New Foodie Romances
items.summary:
There’s nothing I love more than good food in a romance novel. An “om-nom rom-com”, if you will. Thanksgiving, arguably the foodiest of food holidays, is right around the corner. It’s also a holiday that amps up many people’s stress levels. So why not relax with a good book, preferably one that can also help get your stomach rumbling with some delicious food descriptions?

Disappointingly, 2026 has not been the year of the foodie romance. I don’t know if this is a “thin is in” indicator or if publishers thought the market was oversaturated with books about sexy chefs and brawny bakers. But instead of restaurant romances, this year we got love stories about athletes (too many protein shakes), ghosts and grim reapers (who notably don’t eat), reality TV shows, boats, and reality TV shows set on boats. Don’t fear, om-nom rom-com lovers! I’ve sniffed out the best foodie romances of 2026 to help you work up an appetite.

New Foodie Romances: 2026 Edition 

Yes, Chef by Grace Reilly 
 After losing his temper while working at a fancy NYC restaurant full of diners, Chef Jack got fired and publicly embarrassed. Revamping his mentor’s restaurant in the small Florida town where he grew up could help Jack rebrand. But he’ll need some help from someone with serious PR chops. Enter Poppy, an influencer who wants to show her judgmental family what she’s capable of. The trouble is, she’s the daughter of Jack’s former boss — and she drives Jack up a wall. But as they work together, the unexpected chemistry between them heats up the kitchen. If you love dreamy tattooed chefs like Carmy on…

items.title: 3 Picture Books About Sibling Relationships
items.summary:
Siblings are among the most precious relationships that many of us will ever experience. And yet, they do not get acknowledged nearly enough in our books and media. Your sibling is possibly the first friend you’ll make, especially if you’re the younger one. You’ll have to share your parents’ attention and affection with them while you also hold it for each other. They are possibly the only person who understands your family as well as you do, because they’ve been a child in it, too. Even when you fight, it almost reflects who you are back to you, and getting through to them might just make you more aware of yourself. 

Here’s a list of books that celebrate the intimate bonds of sibling relationships.

Lola Reads to Leo by Anna McQuinn & Rosalind Beardshaw 
 In this heartwarming picture book, Lola takes it upon herself to welcome her baby brother into the world with a story for each moment. There is one for when he cries, another for when he’s hungry, and a story each for sleep time, bath time, diaper-changing time, and more. And the best part is, there’s always a story for Lola as well that they all read together during family time.

items.title: Not-Quite-Cozy Mysteries
items.summary:
For the cozy mystery reader, knowing what to expect is part of the fun. The lighter tone, minimal violence and profanity, limited sexual content, and cast of eccentric characters found inside cozy mysteries make them ideal bedtime and escapist reads. General mystery readers usually expect more grit. Finding the balance between general mystery and cozy requires humor, charm, and openness. These not-quite cozy mysteries explore themes of grief, loneliness, class, and racism while maintaining an atmosphere of warmth. With casts of quirky characters and puzzles to solve, these not-quite-cozy mysteries are ready for you to discover!

Knife Skills for Beginners by Orlando Murrin 
 A bit Knives Out meets Top Chef , this mystery takes place in an upscale London cooking school. When burnt-out Chef Paul Delamare is asked by his old friend, TV chef Christian Wagner, to teach classes while he recovers from an injury, Paul reluctantly agrees. Paul starts to enjoy teaching until Christian is found murdered via the cleaver Paul just used in class. To clear his name, Paul must investigate the school’s secrets while keeping his distractible students on task.

items.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
items.summary:
Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough

In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14.

So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life.

Jaenada admitted to using AI in his Prix Goncourt-winning work. The older white man won after Canadian-Haitian author, and younger Black man, Thélyson Orélien’s celebrated manuscript was removed from the Goncourt and other major prize consideration due to allegations of AI use from a conservative columnist.

items.title: Meet the 2026 National Book Award Finalists
items.summary:
The winners of the 77th National Book Awards —given every year in Young People’s Literature, Translation, Poetry, Nonfiction, and Fiction—will be announced this week in a ceremony hosted by Kyle MacLachlan at Cipriani Wall Street in New York City.

Ahead of the festivities, Literary Hub caught up with (most of) the finalists to ask them a bit about their books, their reading habits, and their writing lives.

FICTION 
 Hannah Lillith Assadi, author of Paradiso 17 
 What time of day do you write (and why)? 

Late at night, because everyone in my house (including my three kids!) is asleep. And generally speaking, I’ve always been a night person, although lately the dawn and its colors have begun to really move me.

Which non-literary piece of culture—film, tv show, painting, song—could you not imagine your life without? 

Well I consider all of these literary, but I’ll give one example of each: Sorrentino’s La Grande Belleza , Mad Men , Rodin’s “Je Suis Belle” (sculpture), The Cure’s Disintegration album.

What was the first book you fell in love with (and why)? 

Madeline L’Engle’s A Wrinkle in Time because time travel! Tesseracts! I think I was 8 or 9 when I read it and I’ve really always been a space nerd, maybe because I grew up in the desert and when I was a kid, there was less light pollution and the night sky was full of stars.

items.title: My Father Is a Hill: On Identity, Inheritance, and Finding One’s Place In a Troubled World
items.summary:
I grew up in an area of Southern California known for the beach, the ocean, the coastline, but my family lived far from the water, high in the hills of Laguna. In our car we wound up, up past parks and horse trails until we reached the end of a cul-de-sac, where our gardenia-studded yard overlooked the Ortega Highway. Nearly everyone I knew from school lived walking distance from the ocean, but my parents had chosen this place, inland, high up on the land. Every day involved this climb in a car, our house so far from the bottom that walking down was a fool’s errand, hiking back up in the heat a death wish.

When I was in my twenties, my parents planned their move back to France. All my mother wanted was to live in a small apartment within walking distance of town. After twenty-five years of driving up and down hills to run errands for her family, finally she would make her way on foot every day to buy fresh fruit, flowers, bread. I loved picturing her in this life.

Instead, my parents moved into a house too big for them, far, far up in the hills of Vence. They moved across the ocean to this other continent, to an area known for its turquoise coastline, its stretch of sea, its rocky shores, but my parents are inland, high up on the land, a small triangle of the Mediterranean vaguely visible from their gardenia-studded yard. They have to drive down endlessly winding curves for more than ten minutes every time they want to see friends, eat at a restaurant, buy a baguette. My mother never walks anywhere.

When I visit, we make our way down and back up the hill, down and back…
items.t: My Father Is a Hill: On Identity, Inheritance, and Finding One’s Place In a Troubled World

items.title: Ocean Vuong on Ágota Kristóf’s The Notebook Trilogy
items.summary:
Walter Benjamin, in his unfinished compendium, The Arcades Project , proposes that true artistic and social innovation will not come from the conventionally linear, dialectical evolution of ideas, but through violent displacement of time and place, an ejection of the subject from the discourse into an elsewhere, so that “[t]o articulate the past historically does not mean to recognize it ‘the way it really was.’ It means to seize hold of a memory as it flashes up at a moment of danger.” In other words, new, messianic ideas won’t always come from the sword being sharpened at the anvil, but rather the sparks that fly out from that process, hot and bright enough to start a fire that illuminates what was formerly invisible in the forest.

It is impossible not to think of that spark in the forest when reading Ágota Kristóf. Born in the small village of Csikvánd, Hungary, to a schoolteacher father and an arts professor mother, Kristóf grew up in a rural setting where she developed an early passion for reading and storytelling. Her childhood was relatively happy until the disruptions of World War II and later political turmoil in her home country set her life on a different trajectory.

The language feels both chiseled and fashioned—and is, at the same time, an artifact of the environment they describe.

In 1956, at age twenty-one, following the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian Uprising, she fled Hungary with her husband (a former teacher) and their four-month-old daughter. Crossing the border into Austria and then resettling in Neuchâtel, French-speaking Switzerland, she…

items.title: How the 23 Oldest Words in Existence Differentiate Us From Our Primate Cousins
items.summary:
Where do words live? As a newly initiated word-spotter, you’re probably keen to rush out and start turning over rocks and looking under leaves in search of them. There will be time for that, but you mustn’t get ahead of your self : for as long as words have been found in the world beyond, they have been found within us, too. Here is a list of twenty-three words believed to be the oldest in existence:

Note that I and we are among them. Thus we can tentatively conclude that our ancient forebears were fairly interested in self-reflection—at least as much as they were in worms, which also make the list. That might not seem too impressive, but ask any of our closest relatives, such as chimpanzees and gorillas, which they care more about, and they’ll say worms every time.

It seems, then, that humans are a uniquely self-aware species. More than any other animal, we think about what we have and what we want, what we know and what we don’t, where we have been and where we will be. Other apes don’t come anywhere near us in that department. In fact, we’ve spent plenty of time looking for evidence to the contrary, though never to any avail.

Language gives us the blessing and the curse of being able to produce and understand an essentially infinite number of messages.

In the 1930s, a couple hypothesized that if they raised an infant chimpanzee, named Gua, alongside their infant human son, named Donald, Gua might acquire the faculties for speech and complex communication. Gua never uttered a single word, though an eighteen-month-old Donald did begin to take on the mannerisms and…
items.t: How the 23 Oldest Words in Existence Differentiate Us From Our Primate Cousins

items.title: What Would William Blake Have Thought of AI?
items.summary:
We have had the word icon for a while, since the 1570s at least in our language, but it has recently been subjected to fairly comprehensive alterations. First came the demotion from object of worship to double-clickable thumbnail; then a profligacy with its adjectival form, iconic , which now refers to anything that anyone has seen before. (A short list of things recently called iconic in the New York Times : the San Siro stadium in Milan, Loewe Amazona bags, skating at Rockefeller Center around Christmas, and the 1941 photograph known as The Last Jew in Vinnitsa .) And why shouldn’t it? Shifts in diction reflect shifts in thought; in a culture as voluptuously imagistic as ours, it seems natural for the icon to be a persistent subject.

But words and images both are subject to some of the laws of scarcity and abundance that set the price of rice. The more commodious a term becomes, the less immediate and particular its effect. And the same principle that tells us that changes in thought become changes in language advises us that the loss of a word’s earlier meaning may mean the loss of a concept. The icon’s concept was always its own incompleteness: that it focused a viewer’s attention on a metaphysical object without pretending to serve as its substitute.

These thoughts passed through my mind in November of 2025, as I visited the Yale Center for British Art’s exhibition William Blake: Burning Bright toward the end of its run. Curated by Elizabeth Wyckoff and Timothy Young, the show disclosed a special interest in the material elements of Blake’s art practice. (Wyckoff is…
items.t: What Would William Blake Have Thought of AI?

items.title: This Week in Literary History: The “Man in the Iron Mask” Dies in the Bastille
items.summary:
This first appeared in Lit Hub’s  Literary History  newsletter— sign up here . 

In 1669, during the reign of France’s Louis XIV, a mysterious man, “whose name is never pronounced,” was arrested. No one knew who he was, why he was there, or even what he looked like: the prisoner wore a black velvet mask at all times. He was held for 34 years in 4 different prisons before he died, on November 19, 1703, in the Bastille.

This is a true story that sparked the imaginations of many writers and artists through the centuries, most notably Alexandre Dumas, who in his 1850 novel The Vicomte of Bragelonne imagines that the prisoner was Louis XIV’s identical twin, and Voltaire, who obsessed over the story , and promoted the idea that it was actually Louis XIV’s elder, illegitimate brother. It was Voltaire (and then Dumas, following his lead) who characterized the mask as not velvet but iron.

So who was the prisoner really? We may never know. His identity, despite the efforts of many historians and writers, not to mention one classic 90s film, based on Dumas’s novel, that “ locks French history screaming in a dungeon ,” remains unconfirmed. All the better for future literary fodder!
items.t: This Week in Literary History: The “Man in the Iron Mask” Dies in the Bastille

items.title: The Sensualist by Gary Shteyngart review – a delectable romp through life’s pleasures
items.summary:
From martinis to capybara videos, the novelist celebrates the little things (some more expensive than others) that bring him joy

In 2024, the novelist Gary Shteyngart flew from New York to Milan in search of the perfect midnight-blue suit. There he chose fabric, before flying to Hong Kong to be fitted for four shirts, and on to Tokyo, where he was measured by master tailor Yuhei Yamamoto and master shoe­maker Yohei Fukuda. A short king (“five foot five and a half, with that ‘half’ doing a lot of work”), Shteyngart dreamed of a fit to disappear his 52-year-old moobs (“my tatas”, “my chimichangas”) and melt the heart of the toughest maitre d’ at the most in-demand restaurants.

And guess what? The world’s finest craftsmen will give you all that – though Shteyngart, who emigrated from Leningrad to the US in 1979, argues that a great suit serves a deeper need than vanity. Trying it on two days after Trump’s second election, “it was the final certificate of naturalization … I couldn’t make my adopted country fall out of love with fascism, but at least I could enjoy my new shoes.” Clothes become an advanced form of self-care.

items.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
items.summary:
From Aristotle on, we’ve learned to see long-lasting relationships as more valuable. But what does that leave out?

In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most.

The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line, in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”.

Continue reading...
items.t: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships

items.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
items.summary:
A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back

Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes.

“But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her

items.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
items.summary:
With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing?

The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time.

Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”.

items.title: 7 Books About Mothers with Voracious Interior Lives
items.summary:
The political project constraining American women, the one that gave us Dobbs , rests on a picture of motherhood as a woman’s entirety. Instinctive, total, self-abnegating, and therefore requiring no compensation, no consent, and no interior life. A reader of feminist theory may hear Silvia Federici’s “Wages Against Housework”: Housework “transformed into a natural attribute of our female physique and personality” so that it could go unpaid. “They say it is love. We say it is unwaged work.” Fifty years ago, Adrienne Rich named it the institution of motherhood—distinct from the experience—and the institution now has a legislative program foisted on us by predators. 

Every book on this list documents a mother who is also something else. Voracious. Desiring. Fixated on a dead poet, a diary, a theology, a body’s capacity for harm. Sometimes in psychosis. Sometimes distracted by thoughts which have nothing to do with the baby. The obsession is evidence of an interior life beyond motherhood, whatever its perils. 

I know this fixation from the inside. Sleepless with an infant, I became obsessed with an ancient mother goddess named Cybele, and I followed her from Galicia to the archives of the Louvre while examining my own Cuban matrilineage. The memoir that came of it is Desire Lines . 

Whether memoir, or essay, or confession, or autotheory, or hybrid of essay and autofiction, every one of these books is a mother’s account of a life that did not stop with the arrival of her child. They are literature first. Their political force follows from their craft. Propaganda simplifies…

items.title: This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich review – jailed in Putin’s Russia
items.summary:
The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordeal

Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.

The opening section of his book about the experience is gripping and rather moving. He recounts his arrest in a sting operation, after meeting a contact who promised to supply him with information about Russia’s military-industrial preparations. Born to Russian Jewish immigrant parents in the US, Gershkovich grew up in suburban New Jersey on a diet of Soviet cartoons and “Krylov’s fables rather than Aesop’s”; he was betwixt and between. When he found his way into journalism in his early 20s – first working nights as an editorial assistant at the New York Times, then getting started properly as a reporter at the Moscow Times – he gravitated to Russia and fell in love with it.

items.title: Broken People Don’t Break the System. Broken Systems Break the People
items.summary:
“America, The Never Event,” an excerpt from The Fleeing Season by Jamie D Brooks 

“We needed to move quickly because of the severe pelvic fracture and damage to the left kidney. It was the bleed, we had to stop the bleed. . . . Somehow, the repair to the kidney didn’t, wasn’t somehow, we . . . I . . . it was the wrong side—the wrong kidney we were trying to work on.”

I am no doctor, but I could tell that the physician’s voice was stripped raw, the way voices sandpapered by anguish often are. I understood that his 20-plus years practicing as an orthopedic trauma surgeon could weather his soul, but I detected much more than the strain of accumulated sorrow in Dr Gordon’s voice coming through my phone. Before I could ask my follow-up questions—there were so many—the fresh river of pain coursing through him gave way, breaching the composure he’d fortified through decades of delivering devastatingly bad news to the hopeful. His tears brought me right to his pain. If I wasn’t careful, I could have been swept along with him in his surging current of hurt. For the empathetic, other people’s pain can be a contagion. I resisted my reflexive urge to comfort with, “It’s okay.” It wasn’t. Dr Gordon had just described a wrong-side surgery: a medical Never Event.

In theory, as the wording suggests, Never Events should never happen. In reality, they do—a lot, or at least a lot more than we’d like to think they do. Hospitals are miraculous institutions of healing, aided by the hands of dedicated practitioners. They also can be profoundly dangerous places, their risks obscured in part by…
items.t: Broken People Don’t Break the System. Broken Systems Break the People

items.title: Exclusive Double Cover Reveal of Two Forthcoming Forrest Gander Titles

Electric Literature is pleased to reveal the covers of The Weight of a Frozen Moment and Dune Lines: New and Selected Poems by Forrest Gander, which will be published respectively on April 6, 2027 by Milkweed and April 27, 2027 by New Directions. You can pre-order your copies here and here . 

The Weight of a Frozen Moment 

From Pulitzer Prize-winning author Forrest Gander comes a poignant exploration of intimate human and ecological bonds. In a small intentional community in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains, two sisters—Maya and Mira—grow up sharing explorations, secrets, and the sense that their lives are unfolding in parallel. But as adolescence pulls Mira away, first subtly and then irrevocably, Maya must remake herself alone: through grief and family tragedy, through a journey to Karnataka to honor the anniversary of their father’s death, and through an ever-deepening bond with the place that helped shape her. 

Strikingly lyrical and quietly devastating, Forrest Gander’s poetic restraint and his detailed attention to the natural world imbues the landscape with a gravitational pull on the narrative. The Sierra Nevada is witness, anchor, and the ground on which the sisters find their way back to each other and to an even more expansive sense of belonging.

A meditation on place, identity, and the strength of the ties that endure, The Weight of a Frozen Moment offers unexpected grace in demonstrating what it means to be separate and inseparable.

items.title: Public Access Afterworld by Jane Schoenbrun review – horror in the TV static
items.summary:
The Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma writer-director’s first novel is a wry, hugely fun journey into the dark world behind our screens

Public Access Afterworld is the first novel by Jane Schoenbrun, director of cult-hit horror film I Saw the TV Glow and the more recent Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma; movies in which screens are a permeable barrier and people are menaced by the uncanny realms that lurk behind them. Here the main character is Bethany Peters, a young trans woman working as a content moderator at a YouTube-like company called GlobalVill. Her job is to watch “offensive, illegal, disturbing videos that have no place on the internet” and press a red button to remove those that violate the code of conduct. One night she sees a video posted by someone with the username JulesPublicAccessAfterworld, a visibly malnourished non-binary kid who reminds Bethany of herself “before her stay in hospital, and everything that happened to her there”. The kid says to camera, “If you’re watching this, David Sawyer, this is for you,” then takes out a razor blade and draws it down their arm. Soon Bethany is off on a quest to save them, in the course of which she will learn that she herself is one of “the crooked”, people destined to vanish into Public Access Afterworld, the world behind the TV screen.

There are several other strands to the novel. A nameless patient at the Saint Thomas Youth Rehabilitation Center tells us about a fellow inmate “going by the name David Sawyer” who spends every night narrating a TV programme about a character called…
